metadata.narrative: Write an analysis of the institution of Roman slavery as it is depicted in Plautus' comedy *Pseudolus.* Using the play as a primary source, the analysis must situate its portrayal of the slave protagonist and his interactions within the wider, historically grounded legal and social framework of the Roman Republic. The argument should explore how Plautus' comedic representations of slave agency, deception, and the master-slave relationship both reflect and subvert the realities of Roman slave society and its underlying ideologies.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Plautus staged Pseudolus in 191 BCE at the Megalesian Festival, a Roman religious holiday during which comic troupes performed in temporary wooden theaters before a citizen audience, and this civic-religious setting frames the play's comic license as a bounded, sanctioned event rather than an unmediated social critique.

The play's own thematic core is "the inversion of social class," since the clever slave Pseudolus consistently outwits his freeborn social superiors, Simo and the pimp Ballio, through improvised deception rather than open defiance.

Historically, Roman law of the Republic classified the slave as res, a form of property subject to a master's dominium, possessing no independent legal personhood and therefore no standing to sue, marry with conubium, or own property outright.

Under this regime a slave's body was liable to corporal punishment, sexual use, and even summary execution, and injury to a slave was reckoned as property damage litigated by the owner rather than as a wrong against the slave himself, a principle codified through the lex Aquilia.

The Twelve Tables further embedded the master's absolute power through noxal liability, whereby a master answered for his slave's offenses by surrendering the slave for punishment, often confinement in an ergastulum labor-barracks, and slaves could only testify in court under torture, exceptions being rare.

Manumission offered slaves a legally recognized escape from this condition through the formal ceremony of manumissio vindicta before a praetor, through the census, or through testamentary grant, and jurists explicitly cite Plautine plays, including Miles Gloriosus and Poenulus, as evidence for the vindicta ritual and its symbolic cap of freedom.

Strikingly, Pseudolus never receives this culminating legal transformation, since his reward for out-maneuvering Ballio and Simo is money and a drunken celebration rather than formal manumission, so the play grants him triumph within the fiction while conspicuously withholding the one legal mechanism that would make his elevation permanent.

The plot repeatedly foregrounds slavery's coercive machinery even as it celebrates trickery: a nameless slave boy in Ballio's household fears torture if he cannot produce a birthday gift, Ballio boasts that beating his slaves "hurts him more than it hurts them," and the courtesan Phoenicium is sold, mute throughout, as chattel between a pimp and a soldier's agent.

A modern literary analysis of the play concludes that Plautus is "not necessarily anti-slavery" and treats the institution as "socioeconomically inevitable," so that Calidorus's rebellion against his father's authority is a tactical manipulation of patriarchal control rather than a principled challenge to it, and Ballio's villainy, not slavery itself, is what the satire punishes.

Kathleen McCarthy's influential reading argues that Plautine comedy functioned as part of the Roman "public transcript," the self-performance of a dominant ideology before an audience composed overwhelmingly of citizens, so that the pleasure of watching a slave outwit his betters served the socially dominant as much as any subordinate spectator.

Comedy more broadly articulated the paradoxes of Roman slaveholding, since slaves belonged to the familia and were sometimes buried alongside masters yet remained legally chattel, and this contradictory intimacy produced a mixture of guilt, fear, pride, cruelty, and envy that Plautus's Captivi makes explicit by showing how easily a free man might become a slave in wartime and a slave might prove nobly born.

Plautus's own biographical legend held that the poet was reduced to manual labor at a mill, a punishment elsewhere associated with enslaved wrongdoers in his plays, and scholars read this tradition as partly generated by the plays themselves, making the clever slave a metaliterary stand-in for the impoverished, resourceful playwright.

Some critics compare the play's temporary elevation of a slave's wit to the licensed reversals of the Saturnalia, where masters might serve slaves at table and slaves enjoyed a "December liberty" of free speech, and Erich Segal specifically argued that Roman comedy's impudent slaves are "imbued with the Saturnalian spirit."

Yet this analogy should not be overstated, since careful reexamination of the ancient evidence shows that the Saturnalia's supposed "role reversal" has been considerably exaggerated by modern theorists following Bakhtin, and ancient sources actually emphasize temporary social equality within firm limits rather than any genuine overturning of hierarchy.

Applied to Pseudolus, this caution suggests that the play's comic license operates the same way, bounded by festival time and resolved by the reassertion of Simo's authority and Pseudolus's continued servile status at the final curtain.

The wager structure of the plot, in which Simo bets Pseudolus he cannot succeed and Ballio bets Simo on the same outcome, transforms the slave's cleverness into a commodity exchanged among free men, so even Pseudolus's victory is absorbed back into a transaction of citizen honor and cash rather than becoming a claim to legal personhood.

The absence of any legal consequence for Pseudolus's deceptions, in a society where the Twelve Tables and lex Aquilia rigorously specified property damages and noxal surrender for slave misconduct, marks the play as a deliberately protected fictional space whose comic exemption from the ordinary machinery of dominium allows the fantasy of slave triumph without questioning that machinery.

Read together, the primary evidence of the play and the surrounding legal and social apparatus of the Republic suggest that Pseudolus stages a carefully bounded holiday from Roman slave society's ordinary brutalities.

This holiday borrows the energy of genuine anxieties about mastery, familial intimacy, and the precariousness of status documented across comedy and biography alike, yet ultimately its comic subversion reflects the resilience of dominium and patriarchal authority far more than it undermines them.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Plautus staged Pseudolus in 191 BCE at the Megalesian Festival, a Roman religious holiday during which comic troupes performed in temporary wooden theaters before a citizen audience, and this civic-religious setting matters because it frames the play's comic license as a bounded, sanctioned event rather than an unmediated social critique.

The play's central conceit is thematized by its own study guides as "the inversion of social class," since the clever slave Pseudolus consistently outwits his freeborn social superiors, Simo and the pimp Ballio, through improvised deception rather than open defiance.

Historically, Roman law of the Republic classified the slave as res, a form of property subject to a master's dominium, possessing no independent legal personhood and therefore no standing to sue, marry with conubium, or own property outright.

Under this regime a slave's body was liable to corporal punishment, sexual use, and even summary execution, and injury to a slave was reckoned as property damage to be litigated by the owner rather than as a wrong against the slave himself, a principle codified through the lex Aquilia. [02577_82561]

The Twelve Tables further embedded the master's absolute power through noxal liability, whereby a master answered for his slave's offenses by surrendering the slave for punishment, often confinement in an ergastulum labor-barracks, and slaves could only testify in court under torture, exceptions being rare. [01214_73591]

This legal structure of dominium is mirrored, in an adjacent register, by the pater familias's patria potestas and dominica potestas, since the Roman household head held near-absolute power over both his slaves and his own sons, meaning that Calidorus, though freeborn, occupies a position of dependency on his father Simo structurally analogous to Pseudolus's servitude, a parallel the play exploits when Calidorus must scheme rather than command to satisfy his desires. [05808_10020]

Manumission offered slaves a legally recognized escape from this condition, through the formal ceremony of manumissio vindicta before a praetor, through the census, or through testamentary grant, and jurists explicitly cite Plautine plays, including Miles Gloriosus and Poenulus, as evidence for the vindicta ritual and its symbolic cap of freedom. [00654_69137]

Strikingly, Pseudolus never receives this culminating legal transformation: his reward for out-maneuvering Ballio and Simo is money and a drunken celebration, not formal manumission, so the play grants him triumph within the fiction while conspicuously withholding the one legal mechanism that would make his elevation permanent and real. [05265_65808]

The plot itself repeatedly foregrounds slavery's coercive machinery even as it celebrates trickery: a nameless slave boy in Ballio's household fears torture if he cannot produce a birthday gift, Ballio openly boasts that beating his slaves "hurts him more than it hurts them," and the courtesan Phoenicium is sold, mute and voiceless throughout, as chattel between a pimp and a soldier's agent, underscoring that the play's comic energy operates alongside, not in denial of, real structural brutality. [05265_65808]

A modern literary analysis of the play concludes that Plautus is "not necessarily anti-slavery" and treats the institution as "socioeconomically inevitable," so that Calidorus's rebellion against his father's authority is a tactical manipulation of patriarchal control rather than a principled challenge to it, and Ballio's villainy, not slavery as such, is what the satire punishes. Yet this analogy should not be overstated, since careful reexamination of the ancient evidence shows that the Saturnalia's supposed "role reversal" has been considerably exaggerated by modern theorists following Bakhtin, and ancient sources actually emphasize temporary social equality within firm limits rather than any genuine overturning of hierarchy.

Applied to Pseudolus, this caution suggests that the play's comic license operates the same way, bounded by festival time and resolved by the reassertion of Simo's authority and Pseudolus's continued servile status at the final curtain.

The wager structure of the plot, in which Simo bets Pseudolus he cannot succeed and Ballio bets Simo on the same outcome, transforms the slave's cleverness into a commodity exchanged among free men, so even Pseudolus's victory is absorbed back into a transaction of citizen honor and cash rather than becoming a claim to legal personhood.

The absence of any legal consequence for Pseudolus's deceptions, in a society where the Twelve Tables and lex Aquilia rigorously specified property damages and noxal surrender for slave misconduct, marks the play as a deliberately protected fictional space whose comic exemption from the ordinary machinery of dominium allows the fantasy of slave triumph without questioning that machinery.

Read together, the primary evidence of the play and the surrounding legal and social apparatus of the Republic suggest that Pseudolus stages a carefully bounded holiday from Roman slave society's ordinary brutalities.

This holiday borrows the energy of genuine anxieties about mastery, familial intimacy, and the precariousness of status documented across comedy and biography alike, yet ultimately its comic subversion reflects the resilience of dominium and patriarchal authority far more than it undermines them.
